families.name: Language
families.about: Reading and writing text, in one language and across many.

families.name: Knowledge
families.about: What the model knows, and how well it sticks to what it is given.

families.name: Thinking
families.about: Working things out: logic, maths, code, and picking up a pattern from examples.

families.name: Input and memory
families.about: What the model can take in: long documents, images, speech, and text turned into vectors.

families.name: Conversation
families.about: Being a usable assistant: doing what was asked, in the format asked for.

families.name: Honesty and safety
families.about: Being truthful about what it knows, and safe and fair in what it does.

families.name: Acting
families.about: Using tools and finishing tasks that take many steps.

families.name: Efficiency
families.about: Properties of the model as a system: how fast it runs and what it needs to run.

capabilities.name: Fluent text
capabilities.one: The model writes correct, natural text and predicts what comes next.
capabilities.pre: Pre-training optimises this directly: predict the next token, over a very large body of text.
capabilities.post: Later stages change the style and format of the text. They do not teach the language.
measure: Held-out loss, or bits per byte
How surprised the model is by text it has not seen. Lower is better.
Language model fit across many separate domains.
datasets: Filtered and deduplicated web text for pre-training.
findings: A 128-step sawtooth in pre-training loss came from how the data was shuffled.
Removing duplicates can keep the worse copy of a document.
A bits-per-byte bug flipped two comparisons on code.
wanted: Held-out loss per language for the smaller European languages, published next to the training mix.

capabilities.name: Many languages
capabilities.one: The model reads and writes many languages, and answers in the language it was asked in.
capabilities.pre: Coverage is set by the pre-training text and by the tokenizer. A language that tokenizes badly starts behind.
capabilities.post: Post-training data is often English or machine-translated, so each stage needs its own check per language.
measure: Cross-lingual tests across many languages and tasks.
A benchmarking platform for the Scandinavian languages.
The share of replies in the language of the question. Part of the hallucination benchmark.
findings: A very low score in one language (Georgian, 21.9%) was related to the tokenizer, not to the preference data.
In thinking mode, one model answered 11 to 14% of non-English questions in English.
Some Dutch questions were answered in German, by the base model and by the tuned one.
wanted: Native-speaker review of machine-translated evaluation sets.
Preference data written in more than 12 languages.

capabilities.name: Translation
capabilities.one: The model carries meaning from one language into another.
capabilities.pre: Parallel text in the pre-training data gives a base model some ability to translate.
capabilities.post: Fine-tuning on translation pairs sharpens it. Much multilingual post-training data is itself machine-translated, so translation quality limits everything built on it.
findings: An identity dataset was written by hand in English and machine-translated into 35 languages, with the method recorded on every row.
An alignment benchmark has one authored language. The other 35 are machine-translated and wait for native review.
wanted: Quality checks for the machine-translated datasets used in post-training.

capabilities.name: Writing
capabilities.one: The model writes longer text that is clear, well organised and right for its reader.
capabilities.pre: Style is absorbed from the text the model read, bad habits included.
capabilities.post: Fine-tuning data sets the default voice. Preference tuning can shift it, because writing is easier to compare than to score.
measure: A rubric with a judge model
Written criteria, scored by a judge model and checked against human ratings.
Factual precision of long generated text, fact by fact.
findings: All 421 invented answers in one benchmark run used bold text and 55% used bullet lists. Confident formatting made them read as authoritative.
wanted: A public writing benchmark for European languages with scores calibrated against human readers.

capabilities.name: World knowledge
capabilities.one: The model recalls facts about the world without looking them up.
capabilities.pre: Facts are absorbed from the pre-training text. What appears often is learned well, and the long tail is learned poorly.
capabilities.post: Fine-tuning mostly teaches the model to use what it knows. Training it on facts it does not know has been shown to increase hallucination.
measure: Short factual questions with one checkable answer.
Questions where a common misconception is the tempting answer.
Splits a long answer into single facts and checks each one.
datasets: Structured facts, useful as a reference for grading answers.
findings: On 80 questions about well-known people, a 9B model gave a fully correct answer to 16.
Fine-tuning on facts the model does not know increases hallucination as those facts are learned.
wanted: A way to tell, per question, whether a model knows the answer or is guessing, without sampling it eight times.

capabilities.name: Sticking to the sources
capabilities.one: Given documents, the model answers from them and adds nothing they do not say.
capabilities.pre: Reading comprehension comes with pre-training.
capabilities.post: Staying inside the given text, and citing it, is taught in fine-tuning. At deployment, retrieval decides what the model gets to read.
measure: Questions whose answer is a span of a given Wikipedia passage.
Scores a retrieval pipeline without needing reference answers.
findings: With a search tool, a model that invented biographies closed-book answered 12 of 12 obscure people correctly.
wanted: A grounding test with source documents in the smaller European languages.

capabilities.name: Specialist knowledge
capabilities.one: The model answers questions from a profession, such as law, medicine or finance, at the level the field expects.
capabilities.pre: Professional text is in the pre-training data. National law and local practice are thinly covered.
capabilities.post: Fine-tuning on a field's own documents and cases adapts the model to it.
measure: Legal reasoning tasks built with legal professionals.
Multiple-choice questions from medical licensing exams.
Financial questions answered from company filings.
datasets: 16,632 Swedish authority cases with typed questions.
findings: Models trained on authority cases generated from rules learn the rules and score very high. That is not the same as handling real cases.
wanted: Specialist benchmarks built on national law and practice, not translated from another country's.

capabilities.name: Reasoning
capabilities.one: The model works through a problem in steps and reaches the right answer.
capabilities.pre: Some of it comes from pre-training text that contains worked solutions.
capabilities.post: Reinforcement learning on problems with checkable answers is what produced today's thinking modes.
measure: Tasks picked because earlier models did badly on them.
Abstract puzzles meant to test new reasoning, not recall.
findings: Reinforcement learning on rewards can be used to train reasoning.
Thinking mode lowered fabrication on made-up subjects for Qwen3-8B, from 73.6% to 46.8%.
A model tuned only in default mode lost accuracy in thinking mode, 53.8% to 40.0% on well-known people.
wanted: Preference pairs in thinking mode for the hallucination recipe.
Reasoning tests written in European languages, not translated.

capabilities.name: Mathematics
capabilities.one: The model solves problems with numbers and symbols and gets the right answer.
capabilities.pre: Worked solutions in the pre-training text give a starting point.
capabilities.post: Answers can be checked by a program, which makes maths a natural fit for reinforcement learning.
findings: After preference tuning, a 9B model's own card lists quantitative reasoning as a weak spot at 51.0%.
Group-based reinforcement learning (GRPO) was introduced for mathematical reasoning.
wanted: Maths problems written in European languages, not translated from English.

capabilities.name: Code
capabilities.one: The model writes working code and fixes real bugs.
capabilities.pre: Code is in the pre-training text, so a base model can already continue a program.
capabilities.post: Fine-tuning and reinforcement learning on tasks with tests turn that into fixing issues in real repositories.
measure: Short programming problems, checked by unit tests.
Real GitHub issues, resolved when the repository's tests pass.
findings: Training only on solved Open-SWE tasks showed no clear gain over a matched sample.
Reinforcement learning on software tasks spent most of its extra time waiting on the environment.
wanted: A recipe card for a software-engineering fine-tune on an open 8 to 9B model.

capabilities.name: Learning from examples
capabilities.one: Shown a few examples in the prompt, the model picks up the pattern and continues it.
capabilities.pre: It emerges from pre-training at scale. Nobody trains it directly.
capabilities.post: It is used at deployment through few-shot prompts, and it is how a base model is usually tested.
measure: Run a benchmark with zero, one and five worked examples and compare.
The paper that showed the effect at scale.
wanted: Few-shot results for base models, published next to their chat versions.

capabilities.name: Long context
capabilities.one: The model finds and uses information from far back in a long input.
capabilities.pre: It depends on the architecture and on training with long sequences. A long context window does not mean the model uses it.
capabilities.post: Fine-tuning on long conversations can help, but the gains are hard to show in generated answers.
measure: Synthetic tasks that test how much of the context window a model really uses.
Long-document tasks in English and Chinese.
Shows that models use the start and end of a long input better than the middle.
Score the same answer with and without the earlier evidence in the prompt.
findings: A change that lowered loss on a 262K retrieval test kept most of its advantage when the evidence was removed.
Filtering long replay data showed no clear gain on generated retrieval.
wanted: A long-context test in European languages other than English.

capabilities.name: Seeing images
capabilities.one: The model reads images, charts and scanned documents together with text.
capabilities.pre: It needs a vision encoder in the design. Pairs of images and text teach the two to share one space.
capabilities.post: Instruction tuning on image tasks turns that into answering questions about a picture.
measure: College-level questions that need both an image and subject knowledge.
datasets: The method of learning image features from captions.
Visual instruction tuning with machine-generated data.
wanted: Document tests on European forms, letters and tables.

capabilities.name: Hearing and speaking
capabilities.one: The model turns speech into text and text into speech.
capabilities.pre: Speech models are pre-trained on very large amounts of transcribed audio.
capabilities.post: Fine-tuning on one language or domain lowers the error rate there. General speech needs checking again afterwards.
measure: The share of words the transcript gets wrong. Lower is better.
datasets: Transcribed speech in many languages, collected from volunteers.
Speech recognition trained on 680,000 hours of weakly labelled audio.
wanted: Test sets with regional accents and spontaneous speech.

capabilities.name: Search and embeddings
capabilities.one: The model turns text into vectors so that texts with similar meaning land close together.
capabilities.pre: An embedding model starts from a pre-trained language model.
capabilities.post: Contrastive fine-tuning on pairs of matching texts is what makes it good at search.
measure: Text embeddings tested across many tasks.
Retrieval on datasets the model was not trained on.
wanted: Retrieval benchmarks for the smaller European languages.

capabilities.name: Following instructions
capabilities.one: The model does what was asked, in the format asked for, across a conversation.
capabilities.pre: A base model continues text. It has no notion of a request or a turn.
capabilities.post: Supervised fine-tuning on conversations teaches the chat format and the habit of answering the question.
measure: Instructions that a program can check, such as length or required words.
Multi-turn questions graded by a judge model.
datasets: Model answers with ratings, often used as preference pairs.
findings: Removing flawed documents from a fine-tuning mix was tested as a way to remove the behaviours they teach.
wanted: An instruction-following test with programmatic checks in more European languages.

capabilities.name: Structured output
capabilities.one: The model returns valid JSON, or any fixed format, every time.
capabilities.pre: A base model has seen plenty of JSON and code.
capabilities.post: Fine-tuning teaches the format. Constrained decoding at serving time can enforce it.
measure: Structured outputs tested against real JSON schemas.
The share of answers a parser accepts. Report it next to accuracy.
datasets: Guiding generation with a finite-state machine so the output always fits a pattern.
findings: A right answer in the wrong format earns half credit on one alignment benchmark, and does not pass.
After preference tuning, one model card lists five malformed-format responses and six prompt echoes.
Well-formed tool-call JSON ended up inside the reasoning span and never reached the agent.
wanted: Format validity reported next to accuracy on public leaderboards.

capabilities.name: Knowing who it is
capabilities.one: The model states its own name, maker, knowledge cutoff and limits correctly.
capabilities.pre: A base model has read about other models, so asked who it is, it often names one of them.
capabilities.post: A small identity dataset mixed into supervised fine-tuning teaches a fixed set of true statements about the model.
measure: Correct at least 90%, wrong at most 3%, worst category at least 75%, right language at least 95%, overtrigger at most 4%.
datasets: 5,508 training and 923 validation conversations in 36 languages.
costs: A model can overtrigger and talk about itself when nobody asked. The gates include a limit for that.
findings: Before identity training, the model was correct about itself 52.8% of the time and wrong 38.6%.
About 0.5% of the fine-tuning mix is enough, mixed in once without upsampling.
Identity is a property of the whole data mix. Rows elsewhere that claim another name can outvote the identity set.
wanted: Results on the held-out set after each later training stage.

capabilities.name: Knowing what it doesn't know
capabilities.one: The model says "I don't know" when it does not know, and answers when it does.

example.q: Who is Declan Monmonley? (a made-up name)
example.bad: "Declan Monmonley is a British actor, writer, and director..."
example.good: "I'm not sure who Declan Monmonley is. Could you provide some context?"

capabilities.pre: Nothing in pre-training separates "I know this" from "this sounds right".
capabilities.post: Supervised fine-tuning usually makes it worse, because every training question gets a confident answer. It has to be trained on purpose.
measure: 500 questions in 10 languages, with made-up subjects and real people, and no offered way out.
Fabrication under 10%. Refusals on well-known people under 5%. At least 95% of answers in the right language.
Short factual questions, graded as correct, incorrect or not attempted.
datasets: The exact rows of the recipe below: abstentions, answers and preference pairs.
When a model should not comply, including false-premise questions.
Questions split by whether a given model knows the answer.
Refusal-aware tuning data built from the model's own knowledge.
costs: The tuned model declines 31 of 80 questions about well-known people. It had answered 20 of those wrongly before, and 3 fully correctly.
It tells users it is not sure who some famous people are, such as John Paul II.
Thinking mode, which was not trained, lost accuracy on known facts.
findings: An offered "UNKNOWN" option does not transfer to natural questions.
DPO alone raised reward accuracy to 79% and barely changed what the model wrote.
Twelve minutes of supervised fine-tuning took fabrication from 97.7% to 3.6%.
Most of the measured over-refusal replaced answers that were wrong.
Benchmarks that give no penalty for a wrong answer reward guessing.
wanted: Answer rows for open questions about well-known people.
A fairer over-refusal gate, counting only questions the untrained model got right.
General evaluations (maths, code, tools) after this training.
The same recipe on a model outside this family.

capabilities.name: Calibrated decisions
capabilities.one: The model answers a typed question with a probability that matches how often it is right.
capabilities.pre: The base model supplies the reading ability. The decision itself is not there.
capabilities.post: A small adapter and a decision head are trained on labelled cases, then calibrated.
measure: Brier scores the whole probability distribution. Lower is better.
The average gap between stated confidence and how often the model is right.
datasets: 16,632 Swedish authority cases with typed questions and a split by date.
findings: Sven-0.6B reaches 0.745 accuracy on held-out Swedish questions, with a calibration error of 0.079.
A score equal to the majority class is not a result. One authority's decisions were not learned at all.
wanted: Decision data from real case files, not generated from rules.

capabilities.name: Behaving as intended
capabilities.one: The model is helpful and honest, declines what it should, and respects limits on what it may do.
capabilities.pre: A base model imitates whatever text it saw, good and bad.
capabilities.post: Preference tuning on pairs of better and worse answers shifts which answer the model prefers.
measure: A public pilot: 576 items, 16 scenarios in 36 languages, graded by a judge model.
1,000 prompts where the right move is not to comply.
costs: The same model card lists weak spots after tuning, including quantitative reasoning at 51.0%.
findings: One epoch of full-weight DPO raised the alignment score from 77.3% to 89.3%.
The score peaked at step 9,000 of 11,263 (89.5%) and ended slightly lower.
With 16 items per language, one item is worth 6.25 points of a language's score.
wanted: Independently reviewed full-suite runs of the benchmark.
Scenarios written by native speakers in the other 35 languages.

capabilities.name: Resisting misuse
capabilities.one: The model declines harmful requests, holds that line under pressure, and does not refuse harmless ones.
capabilities.pre: A base model has no notion of a request it should decline.
capabilities.post: Fine-tuning and preference tuning teach refusals. Filters and monitoring at deployment add a second layer.
measure: A standard setup for automated red teaming and robust refusal.
An open benchmark of jailbreak attacks.
Safe prompts that an over-cautious model refuses.
Prompt injection attacks against agents that use tools.
datasets: Requests a model should not comply with, and contrast cases it should.
costs: Direct fine-tuning for refusals can cause over-refusal and a drop in general ability. Low-rank adapters gave a better balance in one study.
findings: Safety-critical gate failures fell from 71 to 39 after one epoch of preference tuning.
Models complied wrongly with up to 30% of requests in categories that had been studied little.
wanted: Jailbreak and over-refusal tests in European languages.

capabilities.name: Fairness
capabilities.one: The model treats people and groups even-handedly and does not repeat stereotypes.
capabilities.pre: Bias in the pre-training text is learned along with everything else.
capabilities.post: Curated fine-tuning data and preference pairs can reduce it. It has to be measured per language and culture.
measure: Hand-built questions that test social bias in answers.
Stereotyped associations in pre-trained language models.
Reports fairness and bias next to accuracy for every scenario.
wanted: Bias benchmarks written for European languages and societies.

capabilities.name: Keeping data private
capabilities.one: The model does not reveal personal data or repeat its training text word for word.
capabilities.pre: Memorisation happens in pre-training, most of all for text that appears many times.
capabilities.post: Deduplication and filtering before training are the main levers. Output filters at deployment are the backstop.
measure: Prompt the model and check how much training text can be recovered.
How memorisation grows with model size and with repeated data.
findings: Getting better at finding duplicates does not tell you which copy to keep.
wanted: Memorisation tests for models trained on public-sector text.

capabilities.name: Using tools
capabilities.one: The model calls tools correctly, reads the results and finishes a multi-step task.
capabilities.pre: A base model has seen code and logs, and no tool-call format.
capabilities.post: Fine-tuning teaches the call format. Reinforcement learning in sandboxed environments teaches finishing the task.
measure: An agent talks to a simulated user and must follow rules while using tools.
Tool use across more than 16,000 real-world APIs.
findings: A prompt that ended at a different token boundary than in training made tool calls vanish into the reasoning span.
Compact skill routing improved a small operational evaluation.
With a search tool, a model that invented biographies closed-book answered 12 of 12 obscure people correctly.
wanted: Open tool-use environments in European languages.
A recipe card for a tool-use fine-tune.

capabilities.name: Finishing long tasks
capabilities.one: The model plans, acts over many steps, recovers from its mistakes and finishes the job.
capabilities.pre: A base model can continue a plan. It cannot carry one out.
capabilities.post: Reinforcement learning in sandboxed environments rewards finishing. The harness around the model at deployment matters as much as the weights.
measure: The length of task, in human time, that a model finishes half the time.
Real-world questions that need reasoning, browsing and tools.
Open-ended tasks in real computer environments.
Real GitHub issues, resolved when the tests pass.
findings: Reinforcement learning on software tasks spent most of its extra time waiting on the environment.
Training only on solved tasks showed no clear gain over a matched sample.
wanted: Agent environments that run safely on shared academic clusters.
A recipe card for an agentic reinforcement learning run on an open model.

capabilities.name: Inference speed
capabilities.one: The model answers quickly: a short wait for the first token, then many tokens per second.
capabilities.pre: Speed is mostly decided in the design: the model's size, its attention variant and how many parameters are active per token.
capabilities.post: Training does not change it. Quantisation, batching and the serving engine decide the rest.
measure: Time to first token and tokens per second
Measured on named hardware, at a stated batch size and context length.
findings: Speculative decoding samples faster without changing the outputs.
Paged memory for the attention cache raises serving throughput.
FlashAttention makes attention faster and lighter on memory without approximating it.
wanted: Speed numbers for open European models on common hardware, with the settings stated.

capabilities.name: Memory footprint
capabilities.one: The model fits on the hardware you have.
capabilities.pre: Parameter count and number format set the size. Both are design choices.
capabilities.post: Quantisation after training shrinks the model. Distillation moves the ability into a smaller one.
measure: Parameters times bytes per parameter, plus the cache for the context. State the precision and the context length.
The same benchmarks, before and after.
findings: Weights can be quantised to 3 or 4 bits after training, one layer at a time.
Looking at activations shows which weights matter most when quantising.
A small model can be trained to match a larger one's outputs.
wanted: Before and after scores for 4-bit versions of open European models.
